I have found a new use for AI: as a tool to identify what motivated reasoning
would look like.   Here's an example from biblical scholarship.

## The problem

I was listening to [Mark
Goodacre's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Goodacre) [NT pod
interview](https://podacre.blogspot.com/2021/06/nt-pod-98-origins-of-early-christian.html)
with [Robyn Walsh](https://robynfaithwalsh.com).

Walsh was discussing her 2021 book [The Origins of Early Christian
Literature](The Origins of Early Christian Literature) in which she proposes
that the Synoptic Gospels (Mark, Matthew, Luke) should best be seen as
instances of classical Greek literary works by ["elite cultural
producers"](https://www.ancientjewreview.com/read/2021/9/8/ajr-conversations-i-the-origins-of-early-christian-literature).

The thesis seemed extraordinarily anti-historical to me, and to probe my
instincts on this, I turned to AI.

## AI as diagnostic tool for motivated reasoning

You can see the whole conversation
[here](https://share.gemini.google/3Mk2isULwXWf).

I started thus:

> Let us say that I was scholar of classics, trained in classical Greek
literature, and I wanted to generate a model of the early church and the
influence of Jesus, that was dominated by factors within my educational
expertise. What kind of model would you recommend?

You can see the response and the subsequent conversation in the full log linked
above. I responded by offering my worries, as a classical scholar, that others
might object to my thesis on various grounds.  Later in the conversation:

> I'm still worried though. However characterized, we have, surely, a quite
unprecedented situation here, where a literary movement goes from invisible, to
threatening Roman civic society, within roughly 40 years. I have to posit that
Paul was - contrary to his claims - a first mover in a movement that was
primarily literary, and that Mark, soon afterwards, produced a fully-formed,
elaborate bios, followed by other major literary successes, such as the other
Gospels and letters - but where - for some reason - this movement was - at the
time, by its critics, specifically identified as being not-literate. Isn't that
going to be too much of a stretch?

To which the AI rather reasonably responded:

> You are right to feel uneasy—because as you’ve laid it out, that thesis has
backed itself into a logical corner.
>
> To make that specific version of the model work, you would have to maintain
four historically contradictory premises simultaneously:
>
> * The "Paul as First-Mover" Paradox: You must claim Paul secretly invented
>   a literary movement from scratch, while ignoring his own explicit, earliest
>   written testimony (Galatians 1–2, 1 Corinthians 15:3) that he was actually
>   joining, persecuting, and then inheriting an already existing network
>   centered in Jerusalem and Damascus.
> * The "Instant Masterpiece" Paradox: You must claim that Mark—writing in
>   lower-register, fast-paced Koine Greek—spontaneously produced a fully formed,
>   universally captivating, multi-layered bios out of thin air in under
>   a decade, without any substantial prior narrative tradition or structural
>   precedent.
> * The "Invisible High-Literary Revolution" Paradox: You must explain how an
>   exclusively literary movement achieved explosive Mediterranean-wide growth
>   among non-elite masses faster than almost any other movement in antiquity,
>   while somehow leaving no trace of the aristocratic, highly educated literary
>   salons that typically produce and consume such works.
> * The "Blind Critics" Paradox: You must explain why sophisticated 2nd-century
>   pagan opponents (like Celsus, Lucian, and Porphyry)—who were trained in
>   classical literary criticism and eager to dismantle the movement—unanimously
>   characterized Christians not as a rival literary movement, but as an
>   uneducated, text-obsessed cult of "cobblers, weavers, and slaves."

It then continues its attempt to rescue the premise.  Read the full log to see
if you find that attempt convincing.
